rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surrounding world and human nature, along with accounts of earlier nations, attest to punishment; deniers insist on seeing it, although the Qur’an already fully serves to educate and remind them.
rows.anchor: This Qur’ān is fully equipped to fulfil this purpose.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi rejects the idea that taysīr makes the Qur’an bland, only for recitation or memorization, or transparently understood by anyone with rudimentary Arabic; that misconception blocks reflection and access.
rows.anchor: every person who even has a vague and rudimentary knowledge of Arabic can fluently understand the Qur’ ān.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One aspect of taysīr is clear, eloquent Quraysh Arabic, neither garbled nor muddled, so Arabs could understand the message and had no excuse to deny God’s truth.
rows.anchor: It was set forth in the eloquent and articulate pure language of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gradual revelation let the Prophet teach and recite the Qur’an over time so people could hear, understand, and absorb it; one instalment, as disbelievers demanded, would oppose taysīr.
rows.anchor: the Almighty revealed the Qur’ ān piecemeal so that the Prophet (sws) could gradually teach it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basic teachings first came in concise, comprehensive verses and short surahs, aiding memorization, understanding, practice, and transmission; fuller explanation followed after people grew accustomed to the Qur’an.
rows.anchor: all the basic teachings of the Qur’ ān were initially revealed in concise and succint verses and sentences

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A teaching repeated in varied styles, contexts, and backgrounds can be understood elsewhere when one presentation or argument is unclear; the Qur’an calls this variety taṣrīf.
rows.anchor: The Qur’ān has called this variety and diversity in its expression as taṣrīf

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi describes seven groups of Makkan and Madinan surahs, with related yet distinct group contents; each surah has a counterpart whose paired discussion complements it, an arrangement made to facilitate taysīr.
rows.anchor: Each sūrah has a counterpart and both members of a pair complement one another in the discussion of a topic.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ‘Ād, Thamūd, Lot’s people, and Pharaoh narratives follow Noah’s example for the same admonitory purpose; Islahi says each ends with the recurring refrain from Noah’s story.
rows.anchor: Each of these anecdotes ends on the repetitive verse with which the anecdote of Noah (sws) ended.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punishment for immediate addressees who deny a messenger is abiding: believers are sifted out, while the deniers are destroyed where they live.
rows.anchor: While the believers were sifted out from the area, those who had denied their messenger were destroyed at that place.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word rendered as abiding points to punishment that permanently takes hold of its location, rather than passing like a gust of wind.
rows.anchor: not momentary like a gust of wind; it took permanent hold of the place it was sent to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verse 40 is the refrain repeated after the prophetic narratives, as Islahi explained earlier.
rows.anchor: This is the repetitive verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’anic reference to Pharaoh’s āl means his entire nation, not merely his family.
rows.anchor: does not merely mean his family; it refers to the whole nation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural al-nudhur refers to all the warning signs Moses showed the Egyptians; discussed in the Torah and Qur’an, each sign was enough to alert them, but their callous hearts remained blind.
rows.anchor: all the signs of warning which manifested themselves at the hands of Moses (sws) to warn the Egyptians of the wrath of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing description portrays God seizing Pharaoh’s people with overwhelming power, from whose wrath no one can shield them.
rows.anchor: someone who is profoundly powerful and potent seizes and from whose wrath no one can be shielded.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section directly warns Quraysh to learn from earlier messengers’ nations: they will share their worldly humiliation and face worse in the next world, while the ending briefly mentions the God-fearing’s reward.
rows.anchor: reward which those who remained fearful to God will receive.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh have no exemption: their deniers are no better than earlier nations, and no scripture grants them immunity; divine justice treats each nation by the same rule.
rows.anchor: It is a requisite of God’s justice that He deal with each nation in the same manner

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their boast that they are a strong group able to fight back is baseless, since no force can resist God’s punishment; when divine might appears, worldly strength cannot save them and they flee.
rows.anchor: No one can resist the punishment of God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reliance on worldly resources makes the proud dismiss opponents’ threats and, even more, ignore messengers’ warnings without understanding how divine punishment will arrive.
rows.anchor: they do not regard the warnings of messengers of God to be worthy of attention.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The routing foretold in verse 45 is worldly punishment; verse 46 points to the still graver Hereafter. God’s practice is to humble immediate deniers both here and in the next life.
rows.anchor: the warnings sounded to them will in reality manifest in the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word mawʿid functions here as an adverb of place or time, identifying where or when the threat will be realized.
rows.anchor: an adverb of place or time here. It means the real place or time

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawʿid means the actual place or time when the threats addressed to Quraysh will come to pass.
rows.anchor: which these threats sounded to them will materialize.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adhā describes a day so ruthless and overwhelming that people cannot take in what is happening around them, each person being gripped by fear.
rows.anchor: that Day will be so ruthless that people will not know what is going on around them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who now claim that accepting a human messenger would mean error and Hell will see that the rejecters themselves were in grave error and ended in Hell.
rows.anchor: on that day, they will see with their own eyes that those who denied the warnings of the messenger were in grave error

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʿar here means Hell, not madness; its plural suggests Hell’s various sections and abodes, as the Qur’an also uses plural jannāt.
rows.anchor: as I have referred to earlier does not mean madness; it refers to Hell.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Being dragged face-first into Hell recalls the sinners’ coming humiliation: their arrogant denial of an evident truth is why they are punished this way.
rows.anchor: This obviously is a form of extreme humiliation.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase mass Saqar could describe what they say or reflect their circumstances; Islahi prefers the latter, as their face-down dragging reveals why they are treated so.
rows.anchor: I prefer the latter. The way they will be dragged face wards will clearly inform them why they are being treated in this manner.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Punishment and Judgment are certain, but their timing follows a measure: God gives everything a defined duration suited to the purpose for which it was created.
rows.anchor: God has created everything with a special measure and set a definite time period for everything

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God applies the same measured pattern to nations, granting a rebellious people respite to develop its good and evil capacities until truth is fully established and it has no excuse; Quraysh receive the respite required by this law.
rows.anchor: If a nation becomes rebellious, He does not seize it at once; He gives it enough respite
